examples: 1980s–90s Pioneer / Sony / Blaupunkt / Clarion cassette decks
OEM cassette units from the same era
one_liner: A wide flat face where the cassette door was, and nothing inside that can hurt you.

price.why: Nobody wants these at all, which is the point.

window_w_mm.why: There is usually no display window worth using — the space is the cassette door. That is an OPPORTUNITY: a flat rectangular hole you can cut cleanly, rather than a small one you must enlarge.

chassis.why: Built like furniture. Also the deepest chassis here, which is the wrong direction if your car is tight.

cage_included.v: sometimes; older units were often screwed in directly
cage_included.why: ⚠️ Pre-ISO mounting is common on this era. Budget for a new cage.

buttons.v: mechanical, large, satisfying, and often not on a flexi
buttons.why: Discrete switches are EASIER to convert to a ladder than a matrix, not harder.

knob.v: often twin concentric knobs — volume and tone
knob.why: The best-feeling knobs of any donor here, by a wide margin.

display_tech.v: none, or a small backlit dial
display_tech.why: Nothing to discharge. The safest possible teardown.

why: The cassette aperture is a big, clean, rectangular hole in the middle of the face — which is exactly the shape the deck's panel wants, and you are cutting an existing opening rather than making one.
No laser, no inverter, nothing charged. The safest category.
The knobs and buttons are the nicest to use, and period-correct for the aesthetic this whole project is chasing.
watch_out: Depth. These are the deepest chassis in this document.
⚠️ Pre-ISO mounting on the older ones — the cage may not be a cage. Check before assuming it drops into a modern aperture.
The fascia is often painted rather than moulded, and paint from 1988 does not survive being worked on.
steps: Remove the cassette mechanism — it is usually one sub-assembly on four screws and comes out whole.
The cassette aperture becomes the window. Back it with 1 mm smoked acrylic bonded from behind and it looks like it was always a display.
Convert the discrete switches to the ladder directly — no flexi to lift, just a wire per switch and a common return.
⚠️ Check the mounting before you build the chassis: if it is pre-ISO you need a modern cage and the donor's own brackets are no use.

models.name: Blaupunkt Bremen SQR 46
models.display: small dial; the cassette door is the space you want
models.note: The cult classic, reissued in 2019 as the Bremen SQR 46 DAB. The original is period-correct and the fascia is beautiful. ⚠️ Price reflects the cult status — you may pay more than for a grade-A donor.

models.name: Blaupunkt Woodstock / London / Toronto (1990s)
models.note: The city-named Blaupunkts are everywhere in the UK and EU and nobody wants them. Steel, deep, and the cassette aperture is a clean rectangle.

models.name: Pioneer KEH- series
models.note: Pioneer's cassette line. Plentiful, cheap, and built well.

models.name: Sony XR- series
models.note: The same story as the Pioneer. Often free with a scrapyard dash.

models.name: Becker Mexico / Grand Prix
models.note: ⚠️ The nicest cassette fascias made, and priced like it — these are sought after for period-correct restorations. Buy one only if you want that specific look and can justify the cost.

models.name: Any OEM cassette head unit from a scrapyard
models.note: ✅ Free or near enough. Nothing inside can hurt you, and the cassette door leaves a clean rectangular hole to work with.

teardown.note: ⚠️ Often PAINTED rather than moulded, and paint from 1988 does not survive being worked on.
Twin concentric knobs on many. The nicest to use of any donor here.
Discrete switches, not a matrix — which makes the ladder rewire EASIER, not harder.
One sub-assembly on four screws. Its aperture becomes your window.
Discharge the electrolytics. Older units have bigger ones.
No microcontroller worth the name in the oldest units.
Steel, deep, heavy. Built like furniture.
⚠️ Pre-ISO on the older ones — check before assuming a modern cage fits.

reuse.value: £12–20, and it is the easiest amp to reuse of any donor here
reuse.note: ✅ The best case in this document. Cassette-era amplifiers are discrete or single-IC, generously laid out, and their inputs are easy to find because there is no digital preamp in the way — the tape head fed them almost directly. If you want maximum reuse, this is the family to choose.

reuse.part: the rear ISO connectors and aerial socket
reuse.value: £8–15 of adapters, and a tidier back panel
reuse.note: The donor's own ISO 10487 A and B blocks and its DIN aerial socket are already mounted in the back panel and already the standard shape. Keeping them means the deck plugs into the car's loom with no adapter and no flying leads out of a hole.

reuse.value: hard to buy in the right shape
reuse.note: On most units the amplifier's heatsink IS part of the chassis casting. If you reuse the amp you get it for nothing; if you fit your own amp board, bolting it to the same casting is free cooling.

reuse.value: a pound, and some peace of mind
reuse.note: The reverse-polarity diode, the input fuse holder and the filter capacitors on the donor's power input are already rated for a car's supply. Cheap to buy, but they are already there and already fused.

reuse.part: the illumination bulbs and light pipes
reuse.note: Filament bulbs behind the dial. Replace the bulbs with amber LEDs and keep the pipes — the diffusers are the hard part and you already have them.
❌ A backlit dial, not a display. Nothing to drive.
